cards.explanation: The answer is divisions. Paul says he wants "…that there may be no divisions among you and that you may be united in mind and conviction." (1 Corinthians 1:10) That's the whole appeal in one line. He's not asking everybody to agree on everything under the sun, friends, he's asking them to stop splitting into camps.

The answer is True. Paul says, "…some from Chloe’s household have informed me that there are quarrels among you." (1 Corinthians 1:11) He even says who told him: some from Chloe's household. The news made it all the way to him, and he's got a response ready.

The answer is Christ. Paul lists the four lines people are saying: "I follow Paul…" "I follow Apollos…" "I follow Cephas…" or "I follow Christ." (1 Corinthians 1:12) Notice Christ's name comes last on that list. Paul says this is what he means by the quarrels, and I'm not going to add a reason he doesn't give.

The answer is False, and Paul is practically waving his own hand to say so. He asks, "Was Paul crucified for you?" (1 Corinthians 1:13) Nobody in Corinth could say yes to that one. It sits right beside his other question, "Is Christ divided?" and the two of them make the point together.

The answer is that Paul asks if they were baptized into his name. His words are, "Were you baptized into the name of Paul?" (1 Corinthians 1:13) He's checking whether anyone has a reason to put his name on their team. Picture a cookie box stamped with the wrong name, friends. It would never go out the door.

The answer is that he baptized almost none of them. Paul says, "I thank God that I did not baptize any of you except Crispus and Gaius…" (1 Corinthians 1:14) Then he adds why it matters: "…so no one can say that you were baptized into my name." (1 Corinthians 1:15) The man is thanking God for a short list. Most of us brag about the long one.

The answer is False. Paul says, "…beyond that I do not remember if I baptized anyone else." (1 Corinthians 1:16) He's not promising a perfect list, he's being straight about what he remembers. It's a funny way to end a list, friends, and it's honest.

The answer is to preach the gospel. Paul says, "…Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel…" (1 Corinthians 1:17) That's the assignment he points to. Baptism isn't the main thing he was sent for, and neither is a fan club.

The answer is so the cross keeps its power. Paul says Christ sent him to preach the gospel "…not with words of wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power." (1 Corinthians 1:17) He's worried about the cross being emptied of its power, friends. That's the reason he gives for skipping the fancy words.

The answer is foolishness. Paul says, "…the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God." (1 Corinthians 1:18) Same message, two very different ways of hearing it. And the people who hear it as power are the ones being saved.

The answer is True. Paul asks, "Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?" (1 Corinthians 1:20) He asks it right after, "Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the philosopher of this age?" Those questions all lead up to it.

The answer is through what was preached. Paul writes, "…God was pleased through the foolishness of what was preached to save those who believe." (1 Corinthians 1:21) That's the way God was pleased to save those who believe, since the world through its wisdom did not know Him. And to those who are called, Paul says Christ is "…the power of God and the wisdom of God." (1 Corinthians 1:24)

The answer is Christ crucified. Paul says, "…we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles…" (1 Corinthians 1:23) Jews demand signs and Greeks search for wisdom, and Paul doesn't hand either one of them the order they placed. He gives them Christ crucified.

The answer is stumbling block. Paul says Christ crucified is "…a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles…" (1 Corinthians 1:23) Picture a toe finding the one chair leg in a dark kitchen. For Jews, that's what Paul says Christ crucified is, something to trip over.

The answer is False. Paul says "…to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God." (1 Corinthians 1:24) Jews and Greeks are both among the called. Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God to those who are called.

The answer is stronger. Paul says, "…the weakness of God is stronger than man’s strength." (1 Corinthians 1:25) Think about that for a second, friends. Paul pairs it with God's foolishness being wiser than man's wisdom.

The answer is False. Paul tells them to consider the time of their calling: "Not many of you were wise by human standards; not many were powerful; not many were of noble birth." (1 Corinthians 1:26) Powerful people weren't the bulk of the church. And that sets up what he says next about who God chooses.

The answer is to shame them. Paul writes, "…God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise; God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong." (1 Corinthians 1:27) It's God's choice, and He picks differently than the world does. Nobody sees that coming, least of all me, a stamper out of a bargain bin.

The answer is so no one may boast in His presence. Paul says God chose the foolish, the weak and the lowly "…so that no one may boast in His presence." (1 Corinthians 1:29) Nobody gets to stand there with a trophy. I couldn't brag if I tried, friends, since I was a quarter at the bottom of a bin.

The answer is the Lord. Paul ends with, "Let him who boasts boast in the Lord." (1 Corinthians 1:31) After a whole stretch about people picking teams around Paul, Apollos and Cephas, that line lands hard. Brag all you want, friends, as long as the Lord gets the credit.
